noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand that polarisation of anions by cations leads to some covalency in an ionic bond, based on evidence from the Born-Haber cycle

primer.text: Perfect ionic crystals assume spherical ions and pure electrostatic attraction, but small, highly charged cations can distort a big anion's electron cloud - polarisation - and every distortion threads covalent character into the bond, moving the measured lattice energy off the theoretical value. This note defines polarising power and polarisability and explains the lattice-energy gap.

lessons.title: When ionic bonds borrow covalent character
lessons.opening: Theoretical lattice energies price a perfect ionic model: wholly spherical ions, purely electrostatic attraction, whole-number charges exchanged once and forever. Real anions can be squashed out of shape - polarised - when a cation drags on their electron density, and that distortion threads covalent character into the bond, splitting the measured lattice energy away from the calculated one.
keyPoints: Calculating a theoretical lattice energy assumes a perfect ionic model: wholly spherical ions with purely electrostatic attractions.
The model assumes a complete, irreversible exchange of outer-shell electrons giving whole-number ionic charges.
Measured lattice energy can differ from the theoretical value.
Polarisation of the anion introduces covalent character into the bond.
The cation attracts electrons from the anion, distorting the anion's electron density.

low.restatement: The maths of a perfect ionic crystal assumes round ions tugging only electrostatically; when a small positive ion squashes a negative ion's electron cloud, the bond quietly gains some sharing character.
low.analogy: Two billiard balls rolling together stay a pure collision; press one ball into a putty ball and the pair starts behaving like one joined object.
low.examPointer: Name the direction of the distortion: the cation pulls the anion's electrons toward itself, never the reverse.

medium.restatement: Polarisation is the failure mode of the ionic ideal: the cation's field deforms the anion's electron density toward the internuclear axis, granting the bond partial covalent character and shifting the measured lattice energy off the purely electrostatic prediction.
medium.analogy: A strong magnet under one side of a water bed: the surface (electron cloud) bulges toward it, and the two objects no longer behave as independent units.
medium.examPointer: The theoretical-versus-measured lattice energy gap is the exam symptom; polarisation and its covalent character is the cause to quote.

check.stem: What does the theoretical ionic model assume about the ions?

options.text: Perfectly spherical ions with purely electrostatic attractions
options.explanation: The ideal model allows no distortion and no sharing.

options.text: Partially shared electron pairs between the ions
options.explanation: Sharing is the covalent contamination the model excludes.

options.text: Diffuse electron clouds that overlap freely
options.explanation: Overlap signals covalent character, absent from the ideal.

options.text: Ions of changing charge with temperature
options.explanation: Charges are fixed whole values in the model.

check.stem: Why can measured lattice energy differ from the theoretical value?

options.text: Polarisation of the anion adds covalent character the model omits
options.explanation: Distorted electron density means the pure electrostatic bookkeeping misses energy.

options.text: Instruments cannot read lattice energies accurately
options.explanation: The gap is chemical, not instrumental.
The discrepancy arises from bonding character, not size drift.

options.text: The theoretical formula forgot a constant
options.explanation: The formula is fine; the ionic assumption is what fails.

check.stem: During polarisation, which species pulls on which electrons?

options.text: The cation attracts electrons from the anion
options.explanation: The positive ion distorts the negative ion's electron density toward itself.

options.text: The anion attracts electrons from the cation
options.explanation: The distortion runs the other way; anions are the polarised party.
No further exchange happens; one side deforms.
Polarisation is precisely that mutual electrical influence.

check.stem: What is the electron-level signature of covalent character creeping into an ionic bond?

options.text: The anion's electron density is distorted toward the region between the ions
options.explanation: Shared-ish density between the nuclei is the covalent hallmark.
Spherical ions are the pure ionic picture, not the covalent contamination.

options.text: The ionic charges become fractional in the model
options.explanation: The model keeps whole charges; reality deforms density instead.

options.text: The electrons transfer completely to the cation
options.explanation: Full transfer is the ionic ideal, not partial sharing.

check.stem: A compound shows a measured lattice energy noticeably below its theoretical value. The best explanation is

options.text: significant polarisation of the anion has introduced covalent character
options.explanation: Distorted, partly shared density releases extra stabilisation the ionic model cannot price.
Defects are a different story; the model gap here points at bonding character.
Perfect spheres would close the gap, not open it.
Full ionic character would match the theoretical value.

check.stem: State the two assumptions of the perfect ionic model that polarisation breaks.
check.modelAnswer: Ions are 100% spherical and the attractions between them are purely electrostatic.
Polarisation is the distortion of an anion's electron density by the cation's attraction, which introduces covalent character into the ionic bond.

check.stem: Explain why anion polarisation pushes the measured lattice energy away from the theoretical prediction.
check.modelAnswer: The theoretical number prices purely electrostatic attraction between undistorted spheres; once the cation draws anion electron density inward, the bond carries partial covalent character and its true energy departs from the ionic-only calculation.

check.stem: A compound of a small, doubly charged cation and a huge anion shows a large theoretical-to-measured lattice energy gap. Assemble the causal chain.
check.modelAnswer: The small, highly charged cation has strong polarising power, the huge anion is easily distorted, so substantial electron density shifts toward the cation, covalent character grows, and the measured lattice energy falls well below the perfect-ionic calculation.

lessons.title: Polarising power versus polarisability
lessons.opening: One property per side decides the outcome. Cations polarise in proportion to their charge density - charge divided by surface area - so small, highly charged cations wield the greatest polarising power: Li+ outguns K+, and Mg2+ outguns Na+. Anions suffer polarisation in proportion to their radius: the bigger the ionic radius, the more easily the cloud distorts, so Br- yields where Cl- resists.
keyPoints: A cation's polarising power rises with its charge density.
Charge density can be taken as the cation's charge divided by its surface area.
K+ polarises less than Li+ because its ionic radius is greater; Na+ polarises less than Mg2+ because its charge is smaller.
Small, highly charged cations have the greatest polarising power.
Anion polarisability rises with ionic radius - Br- is more polarisable than Cl-.

low.restatement: The attacker is the cation: small and multi-charged attackers squash best. The victim is the anion: big, floppy electron clouds squash easiest.
low.analogy: A stiletto heel (small, concentrated) dents a gym mat (large, soft) far more than a flat shoe dents a leather cushion.
low.examPointer: Keep the two vocabularies apart - polarising power belongs to cations, polarisability to anions.

medium.restatement: Charge density is the cation's field strength at the anion's surface: halving the radius or doubling the charge concentrates the pull, so Li+ (compact) and Mg2+ (doubly charged) dominate; anion distortion instead tracks how loosely its outer electrons are held, which scales with radius.
medium.analogy: Grip strength versus slipperiness: the cation's grip (charge density) meets the anion's slipperiness (cloud spread), and distortion is their product.
medium.examPointer: Compare pair-style: Li+ vs K+ is a radius argument, Na+ vs Mg2+ is a charge argument - quote the right variable per pair.

check.stem: Which quantity measures a cation's polarising ability?

options.text: Charge density - charge over surface area
options.explanation: Concentrated charge distorts anions hardest.
Electrons belong to the anion side of the story.
Neutrons carry no charge and no pull.
Mass does not enter the electrostatic distortion.

check.stem: Why does K+ polarise less strongly than Li+?

options.text: K+ has a greater ionic radius, spreading the same charge over more area
options.explanation: Charge density falls as the ion swells.
Both are 1+ ions; size is the difference.
Potassium has more protons; density still falls.
Lithium forms the cation here.

check.stem: Why does Mg2+ carry more polarising power than Na+?

options.text: Its charge is larger, doubling the density on a similar-sized ion
options.explanation: 2+ against 1+ at comparable radius wins the density contest.
Mg2+ is not larger; its charge is the argument.
Neutrons play no role.

options.text: It is an anion with extra electrons
options.explanation: Mg2+ is the cation that lost electrons.

check.stem: Which anion is the more polarisable, and why?

options.text: Br- - its larger ionic radius makes its electron cloud easier to distort
options.explanation: Bigger clouds are more easily squashed.

options.text: Cl- - its smaller radius concentrates its electrons
options.explanation: Concentration aids resistance, not distortion.
Both carry a single negative charge.
Mass is not the mechanism; radius is.

check.stem: The greatest polarising power belongs to a cation that is

options.explanation: Both properties concentrate charge density.
Size dilutes the density even at high charge.
Low charge caps the density however small the ion.
The weakest combination of the four.

check.stem: State how charge density is calculated for a cation.
check.modelAnswer: Charge density is the charge of the cation divided by its surface area.

check.stem: State the relative polarisability of Br- and Cl- with the reason.
check.modelAnswer: Br- is more polarisable than Cl- because its ionic radius is larger, so its electron cloud distorts more easily.

check.stem: Explain why small, highly charged cations dominate the polarising-power ranking.
check.modelAnswer: Charge density - charge per unit surface area - is the measure of the cation's field at the anion; shrinking the radius or multiplying the charge concentrates that field, and the two effects compound in the same direction.

check.stem: Rank Li+, K+, Mg2+ and Ba2+ by polarising power and justify each step.
check.modelAnswer: Mg2+ and Li+ top the list for their high charge density - Mg2+ for its doubled charge, Li+ for its tiny radius; Na+ follows behind Mg2+ on charge; K+ and the even larger Ba2+ trail, their spread-out charge diluting the density.

glossary.definition: The cation-induced distortion of an anion's electron density, adding covalent character to the ionic bond.
A cation's capacity to distort an anion, rising with its charge density.
An anion's susceptibility to distortion, rising with its ionic radius.
The cation's charge divided by its surface area.
